title: The largest of several draws
objectives: Find the distribution of the maximum and minimum of several draws.

screens.title: Both at most 5
screens.prose: Roll two dice. Each cell shows the larger face. We want the chance that the larger face is at most 5.
screens.question: Tap every cell where the larger face is at most 5.

hints.text: The larger face is at most 5 when both dice are.
That rules out row 6 and column 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Both dice must show 5 or less.

byKey.sixes: You tapped the cells with a 6. Those are where the larger face is 6, the opposite event.

explain.text: The larger face is at most 5 exactly when both dice are. That is a 5 by 5 block, $\tfrac56 \times \tfrac56$. The chance multiplies because the dice are independent.

screens.title: Three dice
screens.prose: So $P(\max \le m)$ is a product of single chances. Now roll three dice.
screens.question: What is the chance the largest of three dice is a 6? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Find the chance that no die shows a 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the chance that all three are 5 or less from 1.

byKey.add: You added $\tfrac16$ three times. That counts two sixes twice.
byKey.none: That is the chance of no 6. Take it from 1.

explain.text: All three dice are at most 5 with chance $(\tfrac56)^3 = \tfrac{125}{216}$. So the largest is a 6 with chance $\tfrac{91}{216} \approx 0.42$. Adding $\tfrac16$ three times would give $\tfrac12$, too much.

screens.title: The largest uniform
screens.prose: For $n$ uniforms on $[0, 1]$, $P(\max \le x) = x^n$, so the density of the max is $n x^{n-1}$. Slide $n$ and watch the weight pile up near 1.

derive.caption: With {{n}} uniforms, P(max ≤ 0.5) = 0.5 to the power {{n}} = {{fixed(pow(0.5, n), 4)}}.

screens.question: What is the expected largest of three uniforms? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each $x$ by the density $3x^2$.

byKey.one: That is one uniform. The largest of three sits higher.
byKey.two: That is the largest of two, $\tfrac23$.

explain.text: $E[\max] = \int_0^1 x \cdot n x^{n-1} dx = \tfrac{n}{n + 1}$, so $\tfrac34$ for three. Three draws cut $[0, 1]$ into four gaps of mean $\tfrac14$, and the max sits below the last.

screens.title: Two normals
screens.prose: Now $X$ and $Y$ are independent standard normals. Use $\max(X, Y) = \tfrac12(X + Y + |X - Y|)$, and $E|Z| = \sqrt{2/\pi}$ for a standard normal $Z$.

state.caption: $X - Y$ for two independent standard normals: mean 0, variance 2.

screens.question: What is $E[\max(X, Y)]$? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: $E[X + Y] = 0$, so only the $|X - Y|$ term counts.
$X - Y$ has standard deviation $\sqrt2$, so $E|X - Y| = \sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt{2/\pi}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halve $E|X - Y|$, using a standard deviation of $\sqrt2$.

byKey.zero: You took the max of the means. The max of two draws beats each mean.
byKey.abs: That is $E|Z|$ for one standard normal. $X - Y$ is wider, and you must halve it.

explain.text: $E[\max] = \tfrac12 E|X - Y|$ because $E[X + Y] = 0$. $X - Y$ is normal with variance 2, so $E|X - Y| = \sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt{2/\pi} = 2/\sqrt\pi$. Half of that is $1/\sqrt\pi \approx 0.5642$.

screens.title: Add or multiply?
screens.prose: Three uniforms on $[0, 1]$. A candidate says each is below $x$ with chance $x$. So, they add, the max is below $x$ with chance $3x$.

state.caption: The line $3x$ against the ceiling of every chance.

screens.question: What is $P(\max \le 0.5)$?

options.why: That is the blurted answer. All three must be below 0.5, so multiply: adding gives a chance above 1.
That is one uniform. The max needs all three below 0.5.
That is the density $3x^2$ at 0.5, not a chance.

hints.text: The max is below 0.5 only if every draw is.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every draw must be below 0.5, so multiply the chances.

byKey.b: You added the chances. An "and" of independent events multiplies, and $3x$ passes 1 at $x = \tfrac13$.

explain.text: The max is below $x$ when all three are, so $P = x^3$. Adding gives $3x$, which is above 1 for $x > \tfrac13$. A chance above 1 is the quick sign of a wrong rule.

screens.title: Max and min
screens.prose:
For independent draws with CDF $F$, the max is below $x$ when every draw is. The min is above $x$ when every draw is:

$$P(\max \le x) = F(x)^n, \qquad P(\min > x) = (1 - F(x))^n.$$
screens.question: What is the expected smaller of two uniforms on $[0, 1]$?

options.why: That is one uniform. The smaller of two sits lower.
You squared $\tfrac12$. Use the gaps: two draws make three gaps of mean $\tfrac13$.

hints.text: Two draws cut $[0, 1]$ into three gaps.
The min is the end of the first gap.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac13$: by symmetry with the max at $\tfrac23$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $1 - E[\max]$ by symmetry.

explain.text: $P(\min > x) = (1 - x)^2$, so $E[\min] = \int_0^1 (1 - x)^2 dx = \tfrac13$. By symmetry it is $1 - \tfrac23$. This edge case, $n = 2$, is the quickest check.

screens.title: The density
screens.prose: You know $P(\max \le x) = x^n$ on $[0, 1]$. The density is its derivative.
screens.question: Type the density of the max of $n$ uniforms.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate $x^n$ with respect to $x$.

byKey.cdf: That is the CDF itself. The density is its derivative.
byKey.drop: You lowered the power but dropped the factor $n$.

explain.text: The density is $n x^{n-1}$. Its mean is $\int_0^1 n x^n dx = \tfrac{n}{n + 1}$. For $n = 3$ that is $0.75$, as we found.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Four new puzzles at about 3 minutes each, 12 in all. Keep your own time. Give each answer to four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the four answers.

rows: Expected middle value of three uniforms on $[0, 1]$?
Chance the largest of 10 uniforms is above 0.9?
Expected smallest of three exponentials of rate 1?

hints.text: Gaps for the middle, a product for the max, a rate sum for the min.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Check the dice: face $m$ is the larger in $2m - 1$ cells, so $E = \tfrac{161}{36}$.
byKey.r1c1: Check the middle: three draws make four gaps; the middle ends the second, at $\tfrac24$.
byKey.r3c1: Check the exponentials: $P(\min > t) = e^{-3t}$, so the mean is $\tfrac13$.

explain.text: Larger of two dice: $\tfrac{161}{36} \approx 4.4722$, as in level 1. Middle of three uniforms: $\tfrac12$ by symmetry. Ten uniforms: $1 - 0.9^{10} \approx 0.6513$; three exponentials: $P(\min > t) = e^{-3t}$, mean $\tfrac13$.

screens.title: Follow-up: an $n$-sided die
screens.prose:
You gave $\tfrac{161}{36}$ for two dice. The interviewer asks for two $n$-sided dice. Face $m$ is the larger in $2m - 1$ of the $n^2$ cells, which gives

$$E[\max] = \frac{(n + 1)(4n - 1)}{6n}.$$
screens.question: What is the expected larger of two 10-sided dice?

byKey.top: That is the most it can be, not the average.

explain.text: $\sum m(2m - 1) = \tfrac{n(n + 1)(4n - 1)}{6}$, over $n^2$ cells. At $n = 6$ it gives $\tfrac{161}{36}$, which checks the formula. At $n = 10$ it gives $7.15$, about $\tfrac23$ of the way to 10 as for uniforms.

screens.title: The best of 20 backtests
screens.prose: A researcher backtests 20 unrelated strategies with no real edge. Each scores past 1.645 by chance 5% of the time. She reports the best one.

state.caption: One backtest’s score with no skill: past 1.645 only 5% of the time.

screens.question: What is the chance the best of the 20 scores past 1.645? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: The best is below 1.645 only if all 20 are.

feedback.correct: $1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 0.6415$: the best of 20 looks good by chance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that all 20 stay below 1.645.

byKey.one: That is for one backtest. The best of 20 is a maximum.
byKey.add: You added 5% twenty times. Multiply the chances that each stays below instead.

explain.text: The best stays below 1.645 with chance $0.95^{20} \approx 0.36$. So with no skill at all, the best of 20 looks significant 64% of the time. This is data snooping, met again in testing l12 and validation l12.

ideas: The max is below $x$ when every draw is, so its CDF is a product: $F(x)^n$.
The min is above $x$ when every draw is: $P(\min > x) = (1 - F(x))^n$.
For $n$ uniforms the max has density $n x^{n-1}$ and mean $\tfrac{n}{n + 1}$.
summary.trap: Adding the chances, $n x$, instead of multiplying. A chance above 1 gives it away.

quiz.question: What is the chance the smallest face is at least 4?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The smallest is at least 4 only if every die is.

byKey.one: That is one die. All three must be at least 4.
byKey.add: You added the chances. All three must hold, so multiply.

explain.text: Four draws make five gaps of mean $\tfrac15$. The max sits below the last gap, at $\tfrac45$.

quiz.prose: Two dice. A colleague says the expected larger face is the larger expected face, 3.5.
quiz.question: Is the colleague right?

options.why: The max picks the better die each time, so it averages more than either die.
That is the expected total of both dice.

feedback.correct: The max of the means, 3.5, is below the mean of the max, 4.47.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The max chooses the higher die on every roll.

explain.text: $E[\max(X, Y)] \ge \max(E[X], E[Y])$, with equality only when one always wins. Here the gap is about 0.97.
